strengths: Novel theoretical contributions: Theorem 3 provides a refined Lipschitz bound that explicitly captures attention distribution dependence via max_i||M(P^h_{i,:})||_2, improving over prior work (Theorems 1-2); Theorem 4 is a mathematically solid result on softmax Jacobian singular values using ordinal statistics

Practical approach that preserves dot-product attention: JaSMin is lightweight and integrates into standard training without architectural replacement, avoiding computational overhead and deployment complexity of prior methods
Solid technical soundness: Proofs are correct, the spectral norm decomposition in Theorem 3 is carefully done, and the interlacing theorem application in Theorem 4 is appropriate

Comprehensive experimental validation within scope: Consistent improvements over Specformer baseline on CIFAR-10/100 across FGSM, PGD, and AutoAttack; extensive hyperparameter sweeps (Tables 3-4); effective visualizations (Figures 2-6) demonstrate bound tightness and regularization effects

Valuable insights connecting attention distributions to Lipschitz constants: The observation that both uniform and concentrated distributions can yield small Lipschitz values is interesting for understanding transformer dynamics
weaknesses: Critical experimental limitation for a vision conference: Evaluation restricted to CIFAR-10/100 with no ImageNet validation (standard for ECCV vision transformer papers); only ViT-B architecture tested; no evaluation on language models or other domains mentioned in introduction—severely undermines generality claims

Theory-practice gap in regularization: Equation (3) specifies multiple components (||W^V_h||_2, ||P^h||_2, max_i||M(P^h_{i,:})||_2) but regularization (Equations 8-9) targets only one; Figure 6 shows JaSMin log₁₀ values ~2.0-2.5 vs. exact ~0.6-0.7, indicating the bound remains loose in practice

Unresolved theoretical contradiction: The paper claims both uniform AND categorical distributions yield small Lipschitz constants (Section 3, Figure 1), yet this is counterintuitive given the introduction's discussion of attention sinks as problematic; categorical distribution optimality lacks convincing justification

Modest practical improvements with accuracy trade-offs: Standard accuracy often drops (90.9%→89%, 98.56%→98.4%); AutoAttack improvements are small in absolute terms (~2% on best CIFAR-100 config); no systematic Pareto frontier analysis of robustness vs. accuracy trade-offs

Hyperparameter selection lacks principality: Optimal λ and k vary significantly across datasets and attacks (k∈{0,10,30}, λ∈{1e-2,1e-3,1e-4}); no principled selection criterion provided; introduces more hyperparameters than Specformer baseline

Missing ablation studies and analysis: No isolation of contributions from different regularization variants (mean vs. max, different k values); no computational overhead measurement despite lightweight claims; missing comparisons with recent robustness methods beyond Specformer; no certified defense baselines

Incomplete theoretical justification: Connection between local Lipschitz constants and practical adversarial robustness is theoretically motivated but not guaranteed; why constraining ordinal statistics leads to robustness remains unclear; Theorem 4's ordinal statistics feel somewhat disconnected from main bound application
